meta.title: VSTB: A Camera-in-the-Loop Testbed for Space Vision AI
meta.authorsHtml: Andreas Rebsamen<sup>1</sup>, Matthias Hoefflin<sup>1</sup>, Roger Bruderer<sup>1</sup>, Juergen Wassner<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>
affiliations: 1Institute of Electrical Engineering, Lucerne University of Applied Science and Arts, Horw, Switzerland

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: Validating vision-based pose estimation systems for space applications faces a critical simulation-to-reality gap. Existing approaches are either purely synthetic, neglecting real hardware effects, or robot-based, introducing artifacts from mounting fixtures and backgrounds. This paper presents the Visual Servoing Testbed (VSTB), a novel platform capturing rendered space imagery with a physical camera inside a controlled enclosure. This displayto-camera approach incorporates camera sensor effects (lens distortion, noise, and processing artifacts) without physical mockup artifacts. VSTB integrates astrodynamic simulation, rendering, an FPGA-based camera platform, and web orchestration, supporting data generation, camerain-the-loop testing, model evaluation, and hardware-in-the-loop simulation with closed-loop validation at 10 fps. SSIM analysis on over 4’000 images yields a mean similarity of 0.95, confirming subtle but measurable sensor effects impacting neural network performance. Unlike robot-based testbeds requiring post-processing, VSTB enables uninterrupted closed-loop simulation in a deterministic environment. The modular architecture extends beyond space to other monocular-vision applications.

blocks.html: Autonomous vision based navigation (VBN) has become essential for space missions involving active debris removal (ADR), on orbit servicing (OOS), and proximity operations. Recent assessments indicate that intact objects in low Earth orbit (LEO) now exceed critical stability thresholds [1], rapidly transitioning these missions from research to operational necessities. Spacecraft must autonomously estimate cooperative or uncooperative target poses, a challenge increasingly addressed by deep learning methods showing strong benchmark performance on datasets like [2]. Un-like terrestrial applications permitting iterative real world testing, space systems allow no post launch corrections, making rigorous ground based validation mission critical.

Acquiring images directly from space is prohibitively expensive, which makes synthetic image generation the predominant approach for training deep learning models in space applications. However, before deployment, such models must be rigorously tested and validated. Existing approaches for testing AI based spacecraft pose estimation can be grouped into two main categories.

The first category relies entirely on synthetic data for testing and thus neglects real camera effects, sensor noise, and other characteristics specific to the target processing hardware. While convenient, this implies that models are both trained and tested in simulation, leaving the simulation-to-real gap unaddressed [3]. The second category builds a physical 3D mockup of a satellite or target and mounts it on a robotic arm, which allows testing of the actual onboard processing platform and camera. This approach, however, introduces unwanted artifacts into the images, including mounting fixtures, artificial light sources, and unrealistic backgrounds. Furthermore, even when real hardware is included in the loop, closed-loop testing remains infeasible because post-processing is required to remove these artifacts. Robotic systems are also inherently limited in their degrees of freedom, which constrains the range of testable trajectories and scenarios. As a result, the very approach intended to approximate reality introduces additional artifacts and thereby a new type of domain gap.

Consequently, the development of a rigorous testing methodology that incorporates real hardware into the processing chain without introducing further artifacts, while at the same time enabling closed-loop validation of AI systems in real-time, remains an open research problem.
The main contributions of this work are:

• The Visual Servoing Testbed (VSTB), a novel platform enabling rapid prototyping and validation of AI-vision hardware and firmware for spacecraft pose estimation through Camera-in-the-Loop (CIL) and Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) testing with astrodynamically accurate trajectories.
• A first physical realization providing a closed-loop, end-to-end test environment supporting multiple use cases from data generation to real-time system validation at 10 fps.

• Quantitative characterization of the sensor-induced domain gap through structural similarity index measure (SSIM) analysis on over 4’000 images, demonstrating subtle but measurable effects from the optical pipeline.
• A modular architecture applicable to other monocular vision-based systems beyond space.

blocks.html: The development of AI-based pose estimation models has been driven by publicly available datasets. The SPEED dataset [4] and its successor SPEED+ [2] from Stanford’s TRON facility have become standard benchmarks. SPEED+ specifically addresses the domain gap through both synthetic and HIL images captured under lightbox and sunlamp illumination. The SEENIC dataset [5] extends this approach to event-based cameras, while others such as [6] rely entirely on synthetic images. HIL datasets like SPEED+ suffer from physical testbed artifacts (Figure 1). As noted in [2], infrared markers and mounting holes persist in final images, while post-processing is required to mask robot arms, light sources, and backgrounds, precluding closed-loop simulation. Due to mechanical constraints, robotic systems further limit achievable pose distributions and trajectory variety.

Physical mockup facilities using robotic systems are well established, including TRON [7], ASMIL [8], DLR EPOS [9], and ESA GRALS [10], among others [11]. Recently, [12] presented a dual-robot 6DOF HIL testbed with active gravity compensation, tactile sensing, and AI-based pose estimation for debris capture. While such facilities enable increasingly sophisticated testing of sensor integration, they all share the fundamental limitations described above. Display-to-camera stimulation, in contrast, has a long heritage in star tracker testing. Rufino and Moccia pioneered indoor stellar scene simulation with a display-based, off-the-shelf setup, offering a low-cost and shortdevelopment test environment [13]. The concept was later extended to real-time HIL validation of star tracker algorithms under static and dynamic conditions [14], using an adjustable setup for different test distances inside a darkroom, which served as an inspiration for the VSTB approach proposed in this paper. More recently, such optical test environments have been applied to VBN: Stanford’s variable-magnification optical stimulator [15] uses a lens pair to support both narrow and wide field of view (FoV) sensors, demonstrating far-range angles-only navigation and close-range CNN-based pose estimation, while TinyV3RSE [16] adopts a compact OLED facility for VBN testing. However, these facilities are limited to stimulating the camera in isolation: none integrates closed-loop guidance navigation and control (GNC) simulation with pose feedback, nor targets AI validation on space-qualified processing hardware. Outside space applications, the Causal Chamber [17] validates AI models using real sensors in a controlled enclosure.

The VSTB concept supports the full development lifecycle of monocular VBN systems, from data generation through prototype testing to closed-loop system validation. The system architecture (Figure 2) integrates four components through configurable data paths, enabling the use cases listed in Table 1.

The Space Mission Simulator (SMS) performs astrodynamic simulation and GNC for realistic approach maneuvers. The rendering engine generates synthetic space imagery from the simulated universe state. The target hardware platform runs quantized AI models to infer target object’s pose estimates. A VSTB Control Monitor (VCM) provides a web-based interface for orchestrating calibration, inference, and state management. All components communicate via MQTT [18] in a synchronous loop: each simulation step advances through universe state publication, image rendering, pose estimation, and progression to the next step. Depending on the use case, specific data paths in Figure 2 are activated.

The SMS generates astro-dynamically accurate trajectories while the rendering engine produces corresponding synthetic imagery with ground-truth labels. Both open-loop (grid-based) and closed-loop (trajectory-based) datasets can be generated. The latter is particularly valuable for training recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures, which requires temporally coherent image sequences along realistic approach trajectories. Conventional robot-based testbeds can provide such sequences only to a limited extent due to kinematic constraints.

blocks.html: By displaying rendered images on a screen and recapturing them with the physical camera, the testbed incorporates the complete optical pipeline from lens to model output into the testing process. This enables real-time system testing that captures real-world sensor characteristics such as noise, distortion, and illumination response, without introducing physical artifacts from mounting fixtures or backgrounds. The estimated pose feds back to the GNC unit, enabling true closed-loop validation.

By routing rendered images directly to a software inference application, different model architectures, data augmentation strategies, and quantization levels can be systematically compared in closed-loop simulation. For HIL simulation, the rendered image transmits digitally to the target hardware, bypassing the optical chain. This isolates computational performance and quantization effects from display and sensor characteristics, providing deterministic real-time evaluation on target hardware.

Since the camera cannot be perfectly aligned with the display, captured images differ from rendered virtual images due to perspective and lens distortion. Calibration addresses this misalignment through a two-stage procedure. First, intrinsic camera parameters and distortion coefficients are determined via standard chessboard-based calibration and stored for reuse across configurations. Second, a digital chessboard pattern is rendered on the display and captured. The image is undistorted using these intrinsics, and a homography matrix H is computed from detected corners to map camera-frame pixel coordinates to the virtual image frame. During inference, detected 2D coordinates are undistorted and transformaed via H. For depth estimation, local pixel spacing in the transformed image yields a spatially varying scale factor accounting for screen-camera geometry induced non-uniform projection. This two-stage approach decouples intrinsic properties from testbed geometry, enabling independent camera or mount changes. Validation with rendered test points at known locations confirms sub-pixel mapping accuracy.

blocks.html: Additionally, sensor calibration optimizes black level, white balance, gain, and exposure. White balance uses a uniform reference surface, gain avoids saturation while preserving brightness, and exposure time shall match monitor refresh cycles to eliminate display-induced artifacts.

The first realization of the VSTB concept is a compact, portable unit (Figure 3) housed in a dark enclosure that eliminates stray light for deterministic, repeatable illumination conditions. An OLED display provides high contrast and deep black levels essential for retaining accurate color representation and dark space scene backgrounds. The display is mounted on an adjustable rail inside the enclosure, supporting different fields of view. The rendering engine of the SMS uses Blender [19], with astro-dynamic simulation based on [20].

The target hardware platform comprises an IMX334 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) [22] running quantized AI models for pose estimation. This hardware mounts directly to the enclosure via a flexible flange, containing the complete optical and processing chain from lens to FPGA inference within one unit while enabling rapid sensor exchange for comparative studies.

blocks.html: The integrated VSTB design eliminates external light and environmental variability while allowing independent reconfiguration of display, camera, and processing hardware.

A central hypothesis of this work is that the camera and its optical pipeline introduce subtle but measurable effects on the input image, demonstrating the need for real hardware testing. To quantify this sensor-induced domain gap, a test dataset of over 4’000 rendered vs. camera-captured image pairs was evaluated using the structural similarity index measure (SSIM) [23]. This index combines luminance l, contrast c, and structure s comparisons per pixel:

blocks.caption: Three representative image pairs from the test dataset showing rendered image (left), camera-captured CIL image (middle), and corresponding SSIM difference map (right). Blue regions indicate high similarity, red regions indicate large deviations.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: with

blocks.alt: l= 2µxµy+C1 , c= 2σxσy+C2 , s= σxy+C3 (2) µ2x+µ2y+C1 σ2x+σ2y+C2 σxσy+C3

blocks.html: where µ and σ denote the mean and standard deviation of the pixel values, respectively. The exponents (α, β, γ) and regularization constants (C1,C2, C3) follow [23].

To demonstrate the VSTB system, an approach trajectory toward the Sentinel 6 spacecraft model [24] was simulated in CIL configuration. The system achieved a sustained frame rate of 10 ˙fps, with the camera capturing each frame for pose estimation on the FPGA running a quantized AI model. The estimated pose feeds back to the GNC loop.

Figure 4 shows three representative examples from this test. Although the rendered and captured images appear visually nearly identical, the difference maps reveal subtle but systematic deviations introduced by the physical optical pipeline.

Evaluation of the test dataset yields a mean SSIM of 0.95, indicating high perceptual similarity. Thus, optical pipeline differences are largely imperceptible to human observers. Yet these subtle sensor effects, including noise, preprocessing artifacts, and optical distortions, precisely cause domain gap in neural network performance. This validates the VSTB approach: unlike robot-based testbeds where artifacts require masking due to visual prominence, VSTB introduces authentic sensor effects challenging AI models without unrealistic visual artifacts. The difference maps in Figure 4 confirm this pattern. Strongest deviations concentrate at edges (yellow/red regions), where camera optics and signal preprocessing alter features critical to AI model performance, while spacecraft surfaces exhibit only subtle variations (cyan/green) from sensor noise. The near-uniform background (blue) validates both calibration quality and absence of light leakage.

blocks.html: Table 2 compares VSTB against synthetic only testing and robot-based testbeds. VSTB combines advantages of both paradigms: capturing real sensor effects without physical artifacts to enable uninterrupted closed-loop GNC simulation. The dark-box design ensures deterministic conditions without moving parts, while modular architecture allows independent exchange of cameras, lenses, and rendering configurations. Both VSTB and robot-based systems show limited immunity to external disturbances: robot testbeds suffer from lab lighting and vibrations, VSTB from display color characteristics. VSTB excels in space environment realism via rendered orbital imagery, unlike physical labs. However, the approach remains limited to 2D image sensors, excluding LiDAR or time-of-flight modalities.

This work presents the Visual Servoing Testbed (VSTB), a novel validation platform for AI-based monocular VBN applications in space. VSTB combines Camera-in-the-Loop (CIL) and Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) testing with astrodynamically accurate trajectory simulation. By capturing rendered imagery with a real camera inside a controlled dark enclosure, VSTB incorporates authentic sensor effects without robot-based testbed artifacts. SSIM analysis of raw vs. CIL images confirmed a measurable domain gap despite visual near-identity, validating the need for real hardware testing.

The deterministic VSTB environment supports the complete development lifecycle from data generation through prototype testing to closed-loop validation and its modular concept extends beyond space to other monocular vision domains.
Future work will investigate integrating event-cameras and physically-based real-time ray tracing to further close the gap between rendered and real space imagery.
